france24fr.description: La France "n'a jamais été confrontée à autant d'épisodes de pression de feu un peu partout sur le territoire depuis la fin de la Seconde Guerre mondiale", avec environ 35 000 hectares déjà brûlés, a souligné Emmanuel Macron, en déplacement dans la forêt de Fontainebleau.

france24fr.title: Sénégal : Macdi, le créateur de contenu qui livre des millions de vues
france24fr.description: Avec 9 millions d'abonnés sur Twitter, Macdi est l'influenceur sénégalais le plus suivi. Humour, séduction et scénarios intrigants ont fait de lui un phénomène en Afrique francophone.

france24fr.title: RDC - Rwanda : l'accord de paix de Washington peine à se concrétiser
france24fr.description: Le retrait des troupes rwandaises de l'Est de la République démocratique du Congo, souhaité par Washington avant la mi-juillet, n'a pas eu lieu. Malgré cet objectif affiché, les tensions persistent sur le terrain. Les combats se sont même intensifiés ces dernières semaines.

france24fr.title: Forêt de Fontainebleau : ce joyau naturel frappé par un des pires incendies de son histoire
france24fr.description: Le feu de forêt qui a touché Fontainebleau en début de semaine a laissé la faune et la flore en grande difficulté. Fréquenté depuis la préhistoire et réputé pour la beauté de ses paysages, le lieu est reconnu pour sa riche biodiversité, à quelques kilomètres de la capitale.

france24fr.title: Des ossements retrouvés à l'emplacement donné aux enquêteurs par Cédric Jubillar
france24fr.description: Les gendarmes ont découvert jeudi 16 juillet des ossements, dans un lieu désigné par Cédric Jubillar, non loin du village de Cagnac-les-Mines où son épouse Delphine a été vue pour la dernière fois, fin 2020. Reportage de N.Perez et M.Lassaga (France 2).

france24fr.title: France : les crimes commis sur les mineurs bientôt imprescriptibles ?
france24fr.description: L'Assemblée nationale a voté pour étendre l'imprescriptibilité, jusque-là reservée aux crimes contre l'humanité, à ceux commis sur les mineurs, lors de l'examen du projet de loi sur la protection des enfants. Explications de Flore Simon, chroniqueuse politique France 24.

france24fr.title: Coupe du monde 2026 : les Argentins célèbrent la victoire contre l'Angleterre
france24fr.description: Une foule immense de supporters argentins a envahi les rues de Buenos Aires mercredi soir pour fêter la qualification de l'Argentine en finale de la Coupe du monde. ⚽🇦🇷

france24fr.title: Des ossements retrouvés dans le Tarn à l'emplacement indiqué par Cédric Jubillar
france24fr.description: Les gendarmes de la section de recherche de Toulouse et des techniciens en investigation criminelle ont retrouvé des ossements "qui pourraient être des ossements humains", à Villeneuve-sur-Vère, sur les lieux indiqués par Cédric Jubillar comme l'endroit où il avait déposé le corps de son ex-épouse disparue en 2020.

france24fr.title: Mondial 2026 : l'Argentine, championne du monde en titre, bat l'Angleterre et retourne en finale
france24fr.description: Partout dans Buenos Aires, les Argentins exultent après le coup de sifflet : les champions du monde en titre sont à nouveau en finale, et ce n'était pas gagné d'avance. A Atlanta devant le stade où s'est joué le match, les argentins qui ont fait le déplacement sont soulagés après un match difficile jusqu'à la délivrance finale. Récit de Thibault Franceschet.

france24fr.title: Lecornu en visite au Maroc pour consolider le rapprochement entre Paris et Rabat
france24fr.description: Accompagné de 12 ministres, le Premier ministre français Sébastien Lecornu effectue à partir de ce mercredi soir un déplacement au Maroc. Objectif : consolider le rapprochement entre Paris et Rabat, avec un possible déplacement de Mohammed VI à Paris en ligne de mire. France 24 fait le point en images avec Etienne Paponaud.

france24fr.title: Paris-Rabat : des liens resserrés ? Parlons-en avec Fadwa Islah, Benoît Bringer et Bruno Daroux
france24fr.description: Le Maroc et la France célèbrent leur amitié retrouvée. Le Premier ministre français Sébastien Lecornu est à Rabat avec une importante délégation pour sceller une relation qui s'est renforcée depuis que Paris a reconnu la souveraineté marocaine sur le Sahara occidental.

france24fr.title: L'administration Trump, "une catastrophe" pour les droits de l'homme, selon Human Rights Watch
france24fr.description: Sur France 24, le directeur exécutif de Human Rights Watch, Philippe Bolopion, juge l'administration Trump "catastrophique" pour les droits de l'homme, aux États-Unis comme à l'international. Il l'accuse de vouloir "détruire l'idée même de justice internationale" et dénonce un exemple américain "corrosif" pour le reste du monde.

france24fr.title: "Le bain des Dieux" : Lionel Messi et Lamine Yamal se retrouvent en finale du Mondial
france24fr.description: Le prodige argentin du FC Barcelone Lionel Messi a donné un bain à un bébé, un certain Lamine Yamal, devant un photographe à l'occasion d'une campagne caritative, en septembre 2007. Le destin veut que les chemins du génial vétéran et du jeune attaquant vont se recroiser, dimanche, au Metlife Stadium en finale de la Coupe du monde.

france24fr.title: Mondial 2026 : l'Argentine prive l'Angleterre d'une première finale depuis 1996
france24fr.description: Menée 1-0, l'Argentine a renversé l'Angleterre 2-1 mercredi à Atlanta en demi-finale du Mondial 2026 grâce à deux passes décisives de Lionel Messi, et défendra son titre contre l'Espagne, tombeuse la veille de la France. Récit de Victor Faubert.

france24fr.title: Affaire Pegasus : le Maroc continue de nier avoir utilisé le logiciel espion
france24fr.description: Cinq ans après les révélations d'espionnage via le logiciel Pegasus, et alors que le premier ministre français est en déplacement au Maroc, un consortium de médias français dont Le Monde, Forbidden Stories et Radio France publient de nouvelles révélations, aves des preuves que le Maroc a espionné, à l'aide de ce logiciel de fabrication israélienne, des citoyens ainsi que des dirigeants français. Récit d'Héloïse Mélan.

france24fr.title: En Iran, un motard britannique condamné pour espionnage par Téhéran
france24fr.description: La peine de prison du Britannique Craig Foreman, détenu en Iran avec son épouse depuis leur arrestation début 2025 alors qu'ils faisaient un tour du monde à moto, a été étendue de deux ans, a indiqué leur famille. Lindsay et Craig Foreman ont été condamnés en février à dix ans de prison pour espionnage, une accusation qu'ils nient. Leur histoire, racontée par Emerald Maxwell et Etienne Paponaud.

nzz.title: Frankreich legalisiert die Sterbehilfe für Schwerkranke – doch der letzte Entscheid steht noch aus
nzz.description: Nach jahrelanger Debatte hat Frankreich ein Gesetz zur Sterbehilfe verabschiedet. Ein interdisziplinäres Gremium soll jeden Antrag prüfen, Mediziner können ihre Mitwirkung aus Gewissensgründen verweigern. Für die Gegner ist der Streit nicht beendet.

spiegel.description: Was eine Recruiterin über KI-Bewerbungen denkt. Was man allein auf einem Festival über sich lernt. Und wo Studierende am häufigsten noch bei den Eltern wohnen. Die Texte der Woche zu Studium und Berufseinstieg.

spiegel.description: Nach dem Rückzug von Kai Wegner soll Stefan Evers die CDU im Roten Rathaus halten. In einem Interview berichtet er von Anfeindungen wegen seiner Homosexualität – und erklärt den Kampf gegen Hassgewalt zur Priorität.

phys-org.title: Quantum teleportation could reduce photon loss in long-distance communications
phys-org.description: Quantum technologies, which leverage the principles of quantum mechanics, have been found to outperform their classical counterparts on specific tasks. Among other things, past studies have highlighted the potential of quantum systems that can enable long-distance communication, using photons (i.e., particles of light) to carry quantum information.

However, how such small peptides recognize different proteins depending on their surrounding chemical environment has not yet been fully understood.

phys-org.title: Tiny gene edit cuts cadmium in rice by 48% without reducing yields
phys-org.description: Cadmium (Cd) contamination poses a serious threat to global food safety. As a toxic and carcinogenic heavy metal, cadmium can accumulate in agricultural soils through industrialization and urbanization before entering the human food chain. Rice is especially vulnerable because it absorbs more cadmium than other major cereal crops, making it one of the largest dietary sources of cadmium exposure for nearly half the world's population.

phys-org.title: Roadless rule helps protect clean drinking water for 25 million Americans, new study shows
phys-org.description: Approximately 90% of the U.S. population relies on public water systems. A significant portion of the water supplying those systems comes from forested lands, which means policies affecting forests also affect water access.

phys-org.title: Study finds LLMs nudge users toward smart savings and investing habits—but the guidance skews
phys-org.description: Would you trust a large language model to help plan your financial future? Many Americans already do. In a 2025 survey, more than half said they'd asked AI for financial advice. By comparison, about 40% have worked with a human financial adviser, suggesting that when generative AI talks money, people listen.

phys-org.title: Rare mutations are helping dangerous hospital bacteria slip past the last-line antibiotic defense

The powerful antibiotic combination ceftazidime-avibactam (CZA), widely used to treat severe hospital-acquired infections caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa—particularly in critically ill and immunocompromised patients—can no longer eliminate some of these infections.

phys-org.title: How NASA's Artemis III lander test will pave way for moon landings
phys-org.description: Before Artemis astronauts land on the moon's surface in 2028, NASA will conduct the Artemis III demonstration mission in 2027, allowing teams on Earth and in orbit to practice rendezvous and docking operations between commercial human landing systems and the Orion spacecraft. Data from that mission, along with future uncrewed demonstration missions at the moon, will support astronaut safety and mission success for crewed lunar landings.

phys-org.title: New research shows how to expand the pool of tomorrow's leaders

Many of these fish belong to a lineage known as Scombridae, whose members are characterized by fins supported by thin, bony structures known as rays.

phys-org.title: FIFA and pop superstars should discount tickets for fans to keep climate costs of 'mega-events' down, say researchers
phys-org.description: The vast majority of carbon emissions caused by "mega-events" such as World Cups and global concert tours come from audience travel, according to University of Cambridge researchers. In a new study, researchers estimate that expanding to 48 teams for this year's World Cup increased emissions by well over half a million metric tons to some 4.23 million metric tons of carbon for the whole tournament, 82% of which comes from traveling fans, with around 3 million metric tons from flying alone.

phys-org.title: Frog protein could become first antidote to deadly red tide toxin
phys-org.description: The "red tide" algal blooms that are becoming more frequent along the Pacific coast produce one of the most potent neurotoxins known: saxitoxin, or STX. The toxin accumulates in shellfish and causes paralytic shellfish poisoning (PSP) when consumed.

phys-org.title: Climate change makes extreme West Africa rainfall five times likelier, study finds
phys-org.description: Climate change has made extreme rainfall in West Africa five times more likely than in the late 19th century, scientists said Thursday, after regional floods killed nearly 100 people last month.

phys-org.title: Toronto air ranked among world's worst as wildfire smoke billows south

phys-org.title: Heavy smoke from wildfires blankets the US Midwest and Northeast, prompting evacuations
phys-org.description: Thousands of visitors were told to evacuate a remote Minnesota wilderness area accessible only by boat as wildfires send dangerously heavy smoke over the U.S. Midwest and Northeast this week.

phys-org.title: Understanding Bavaria's Indigeneity
phys-org.description: When I tell people that I am a proud Boarisch-Schwob—Bavarian-Swabian—Indigenous person, I am often met with disbelief. I am white. I am European. I come from Bavaria, one of Europe's wealthiest regions. For some people, those facts settle the question before I have explained anything else.

phys-org.title: When disaster strikes, people often flee to places that feel familiar
phys-org.description: When the Marshall Fire tore through suburban Colorado in late 2021, residents had only hours to decide where to go. Some fled to nearby towns. Others stayed farther away for weeks or months. Now, a recent study published in Humanities and Social Sciences Communications suggests those decisions were shaped not only by distance or danger but also by something more human: the pull of familiar communities and social ties.

But it remains to be seen whether this new approach, which the administration has called “broken” in the private sector, will be effective without causing dangerous delays for Medicare recipients.

undark.title: Review: What Animals Can Teach Humans About Caregiving
undark.description: From seahorses and birds to beetles and killer whales, journalist Elizabeth Preston finds a lot of common ground  between human and animal parenting in “The Creatures’ Guide to Caring,” a sweeping survey of the evolution of caregiving and the dizzying array of survival strategies in the animal kingdom.

undark.title: The MAHA Movement’s Worrisome Embrace of Ibogaine
undark.description: The MAHA movement has been promoting the plant-based substance ibogaine as a remedy for opioid addiction, despite the lack of clinical trials on its safety and efficacy. One physician who practices addiction medicine discusses the risks of ibogaine and argues for the need to support proven treatments.

undark.title: Advocacy Groups Express Mixed Views on Embryo Editing
undark.description: At least two new start-up companies, Preventive and Origin Genomics, say they are developing strategies that combine gene editing with in vitro fertilization to correct disease-causing mutations. Advocacy groups for people living with these genetic disorders have been quiet on the developments.

undark.title: Interview: California Lawmaker Calls for a Peptide Working Group

undark.title: Making Sense of Data From Wearable Health Trackers
undark.description: Wearable health devices such as smartwatches, glucose monitors, and sleep trackers are blurring the line between consumer wellness and clinical medicine. One physician argues that validation standards and privacy protections must be established to ensure the usefulness of the data these devices generate.

undark.title: In California, a Plan to Help Wildlife Cross a Busy Freeway
undark.description: The 101 freeway in California bisects a mountainous region where threatened cougars and other animals are blocked without a viable path across 10 lanes of heavily trafficked roadway. But an ambitious 210-foot “vegetated bridge” will soon be home to what organizers say is the largest wildlife crossing anywhere in the world.

undark.title: Promising ‘Liquid Biopsies’ May Not Be Ready for Primetime
undark.description: Multi-cancer early detection tests seek to spot cancer from a single blood draw. Enabling earlier cancer diagnoses could help save lives and limit the need for invasive interventions. But while the tests are promising, physicians have expressed doubt about routine use by low-risk and asymptomatic individuals.

undark.title: Book Review: How Radio Astronomy Made the Invisible Visible
undark.description: According to astronomer Emma Chapman’s revelatory “The Echoing Universe,” the history of radio astronomy is filled with surprises that have revealed parts of the universe that would otherwise remain hidden and invisible — DIY instruments, secrets accidentally uncovered, and persistent connections to Earth.

proj-syn.title: Hungary’s Real Economic Test
proj-syn.description: Entering the euro with favorable market sentiment, but without an economy that can function well within a monetary union, would not serve Hungary’s long-term interests. It would be a formula for more broken promises—precisely the trend that the new government was elected to end.

proj-syn.title: The Iran War Exposes the Global Economy’s Fault Lines
proj-syn.description: Buoyed by AI stocks, global financial markets have largely shrugged off the war with Iran. Yet the conflict’s long-term economic costs are only beginning to emerge, as depleted strategic oil reserves, damaged refining capacity, and rising fuel and fertilizer costs increasingly weigh on lower-income economies.

proj-syn.title: Governments Should Govern AI, Not Own It
proj-syn.description: AI systems are now powerful enough to threaten critical infrastructure, financial systems, and national security. Rather than becoming shareholders in AI companies, as US President Donald Trump has proposed, governments should invest in the independent institutions needed to hold the industry accountable.

proj-syn.title: The Tragedy of “Westalgia”
proj-syn.description: Some European leaders seem to think that abasing themselves for Donald Trump's pleasure is necessary to save NATO and keep the Western alliance alive. But by so desperately clinging to the good old days of the transatlantic relationship, Europe’s leaders are risking more than just their dignity.

proj-syn.title: The West’s Turkey Dilemma
proj-syn.description: Few countries better illustrate the difficult trade-off between democratic principles and strategic necessity than Turkey. As the country’s geopolitical and economic importance grows, NATO allies are becoming increasingly willing to overlook President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s attacks on democratic institutions.

proj-syn.title: How the Tech Lords Hacked the Firm
proj-syn.description: A handful of tech oligarchs have figured out how to tap public markets without submitting to shareholder oversight. The recent SpaceX IPO represents the culmination of this process, granting Elon Musk near-total authority and revealing how thoroughly the mechanisms meant to hold corporate leaders accountable have been weakened.

proj-syn.title: Asia’s Real Energy Test
proj-syn.description: The Iran war has underscored the fragility of global energy markets, exposing which economies can withstand repeated shocks and which cannot. For ASEAN+3 countries, resilience will depend on stronger electricity systems, regional cooperation, and institutions that can manage persistent uncertainty.

proj-syn.title: The US Economy Cannot Grow Without Renewables
proj-syn.description: Consumption demand, which has long powered America’s formidable economy, rests on the promise of cheap energy. But the Trump administration has conflated that with fossil fuels, confusing historic correlation with causation and, in the process, jeopardizing long-term prosperity.

proj-syn.title: The Purpose of Development Cooperation Is to Be Unnecessary
proj-syn.description: The original promise of development cooperation was to help countries overcome poverty, build productive economies, and reduce their dependence on external resources. That has not happened, and ongoing reviews of development cooperation, which focus on donor countries' needs and priorities, are unlikely to change this.

proj-syn.title: Oil Shocks Are No Longer So Shocking
proj-syn.description: Despite this year's US/Israeli-Iran war causing the largest-ever disruption to global oil supplies, the shocks of the 1970s had a greater impact. Because oil has been used as a weapon for so long, markets, policymakers, and strategists have adapted.

proj-syn.title: The Mother of All Economic Shocks Is Chinese Mercantilism
proj-syn.description: Because analysts tend to put the United States at the center of the global economic story, they have overlooked the single most important force of the past 50 years. But it will be obvious to later generations that Chinese mercantilism has been more globally consequential than any other economic shock or policy choice.

proj-syn.title: Letting Russia Burn
proj-syn.description: From relentless Ukrainian drone strikes to soaring inflation and fuel shortages, Russia is paying an ever-higher price for Vladimir Putin's war of choice. But the war has become the organizing principle of Putin’s regime, leaving no path to lasting peace without a fundamental political transformation.

proj-syn.title: What AI Governance Demands
proj-syn.description: AI governance must account for everything from the technology’s material requirements to its effects on communities, businesses, labor markets, the environment, and strategic competition. To this end, a framework of verification-based trust—broader than national regulation and more flexible than a classic treaty—is essential.

proj-syn.title: A Japanese Wake-Up Call for America
proj-syn.description: Japan’s deepening currency and bond-market woes should be a wake-up call for other countries that appear to be on unsustainable fiscal paths, not least the United States, as well as France, Italy, and the United Kingdom. After all, a crisis in one country often draws investors' attention to others facing similar problems.

proj-syn.title: The Israel-Lebanon Recipe for Never-Ending War
proj-syn.description: Lebanon’s political circumstances, together with Iran’s strengthened regional position, make Hezbollah’s complete disarmament highly unlikely. By conditioning Israel’s withdrawal from Lebanon on this outcome—but with no provisions about cutting Hezbollah’s Iranian lifeline—the new framework agreement is dead on arrival.

proj-syn.title: Why This Energy Shock Is Different
proj-syn.description: Unlike recent energy crises, today’s geopolitical shock is destroying supply rather than rerouting it, exposing the limits of the standard policy toolkit. Governments can mitigate its impact on those most exposed, but only if fiscal and monetary policy work in concert.

proj-syn.title: China’s Erasure of Tibet Is Accelerating
proj-syn.description: In recent years, the international community has stood idly by while China has systematically eradicated Tibetan culture and identity. With the authorities stepping up their assimilation efforts, Asia risks not only losing one of its oldest civilizations, but also facing a China that is bigger, bolder, and more powerful than ever.

proj-syn.title: Judging the Enhanced Games
proj-syn.description: If fairness in sports required a level playing field that all who wish to compete could afford, that would be a reason for banning expensive performance-enhancing drugs. But it would be a reason for banning expensive high-tech swimming suits and expensive high-tech running shoes, too.
